Title: Server CPU utilization above 90 percent
Description: Sustained CPU utilization above 90 percent slows application response and can delay user transactions. Short spikes during scheduled batch jobs are expected. Utilization above 90 percent for more than 10 minutes must be investigated.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the CPU reading on the monitoring dashboard and check that it has lasted at least 10 minutes. 2) Identify the top CPU consuming processes. 3) Check whether a backup, batch job or patch installation is running and pause non-critical jobs. 4) If a runaway process is found, restart only that process after confirming with the application owner. 5) Record CPU readings and actions in the incident ticket. 6) If CPU remains above 90 percent for 30 minutes, escalate.

Title: High memory utilization
Description: Memory utilization above 90 percent can cause swapping, slow applications and out-of-memory crashes. A steady rise in memory use over several hours can indicate a memory leak in the application.
Procedure: 1) Confirm memory and swap usage on the monitoring dashboard. 2) Identify the processes using the most memory. 3) Check whether memory usage grows steadily over hours, which suggests a memory leak. 4) Notify the application owner before restarting any application service. 5) Restart the affected service only in an approved window, or in an emergency with Incident Manager approval. 6) Verify memory returns to normal and monitor for 60 minutes. 7) If swap usage stays high or the server stops responding, escalate.

Title: Disk space monitoring thresholds
Description: Disk space is monitored on every production server. A warning alert is raised when a volume reaches 80 percent used and a critical alert is raised at 90 percent used. Thresholds are reviewed each quarter by the Infrastructure team.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the disk monitoring agent reports every production volume. 2) Review warning alerts at 80 percent on the same business day. 3) Treat critical alerts at 90 percent as urgent and follow the high disk utilization procedure. 4) Record the volume name and free space trend in the monthly capacity report.

Title: Server availability check
Description: Each production server is checked every 60 seconds by ping and by an agent heartbeat. A server that misses three consecutive heartbeats is marked unavailable and a critical alert is raised.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the server is unavailable from the monitoring console and from a second monitoring location. 2) Check whether a planned maintenance window covers the server. 3) Use remote management (iLO or iDRAC) to view the server console. 4) If the server is not reachable, open an incident and escalate to the server operations on-call team. 5) Update the incident ticket every 15 minutes until the server is available.

Title: Application service restart procedure
Description: Application services are restarted to recover from hung processes or after approved configuration changes. Restarts must follow the approved sequence to avoid data loss.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the application owner and the incident or change ticket reference. 2) Notify the service desk that users may see a short outage. 3) Stop the front-end services first, then stop the application service. 4) Check that the application process has fully stopped and that no lock files remain. 5) Start the application service, then start the front-end services. 6) Verify the health check URL returns a success response and test one business transaction. 7) Record the restart time and result in the ticket.

Title: Database connectivity failure
Description: Applications can lose connectivity to the database server because of a listener failure, an expired database account or a network problem.
Procedure: 1) Test the connection from the application server using the database client tool. 2) Check that the database listener or service is running on the database server. 3) Verify the database account is not locked or expired. 4) Check network connectivity between the application server and the database port using the network connectivity procedure. 5) If the database service is down, escalate to the Database Administrator on-call team. Do not restart the database without DBA approval.

Title: Network connectivity troubleshooting
Description: Users or servers can lose network access because of a cable, switch port, VLAN or routing problem. Start with the scope of the problem to decide which layer to check first.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the scope: one user, one server, one floor or the whole site. 2) Check the link status and IP address on the affected device, then ping the default gateway. 3) If the gateway does not respond, check the switch port status and VLAN assignment. 4) If the gateway responds, ping the destination by IP address and then by hostname to separate routing and DNS issues. 5) Use traceroute to find the hop where packets stop. 6) If more than one device or a core switch is affected, escalate to the Network Operations Centre.

Title: Firewall connectivity blocked
Description: Application traffic can be blocked by a firewall rule change or by a missing rule for a new service.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the source IP address, destination IP address and port that are blocked. 2) Check the firewall logs for deny entries that match the source and destination. 3) Check whether a change request modified firewall rules in the last 24 hours. 4) Request a rule change through the approved firewall change process. Do not disable the firewall. 5) Verify connectivity after the rule change and close the ticket with the rule reference.

Title: DNS resolution failure
Description: Hostnames fail to resolve when the DNS server is unavailable or when a DNS record is missing or incorrect.
Procedure: 1) Test name resolution with nslookup against the primary DNS server, then against the secondary DNS server. 2) If only the primary fails, confirm that clients are using the secondary server. 3) Check the DNS service status on the DNS server and review its event log. 4) If a record is missing, request a DNS record change through the change process. 5) Flush the DNS cache on affected clients after the fix.

Title: Backup scheduling standard
Description: Production servers follow a fixed backup schedule. Full backups run weekly on Sunday at 01:00. Incremental backups run daily at 01:00 from Monday to Saturday. All backup jobs must finish within the backup window of 01:00 to 05:00.
Procedure: 1) Confirm each production server is included in the backup policy. 2) Review the backup calendar every Monday to confirm that last weekend's full backup completed. 3) Review the backup duration report monthly. 4) If jobs regularly exceed the backup window, raise a change request to adjust the schedule or capacity.

Title: Backup job failure handling
Description: A backup job is marked failed when it cannot finish copying data, when the backup target is full, or when the backup agent is offline on the source server.
Procedure: 1) Open the backup job log and note the first error message and its time. 2) Check free space on the backup target. 3) Confirm the backup agent service is running on the source server. 4) Check that the source server is reachable on the backup network. 5) After the cause is fixed, re-run the failed job once outside peak hours. 6) If the job fails again, or any production server has no successful backup in 24 hours, escalate to the Backup Administrator and open an incident.

Title: Backup restoration test and restore procedure
Description: Backups are only useful if they can be restored. A restore test is run every quarter on one non-production server to prove the backups work.
Procedure: 1) Obtain approval and the required restore point time from the requester. 2) Restore to an alternate location, not the production path, unless the Incident Manager approves a production restore. 3) Verify file counts, checksums or application start-up after the restore. 4) Record the restore time, the data checked and any gaps in the quarterly test report.

Title: Infrastructure monitoring coverage
Description: Every new server, network device and storage array must be added to monitoring within five working days of go-live.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the device has a monitoring agent or SNMP configuration. 2) Confirm CPU, memory, disk, availability and network interface checks are enabled. 3) Confirm alert routing sends critical alerts to the correct on-call group. 4) Review the monitoring coverage report monthly and raise gaps with the owning team.

Title: Critical alert response
Description: Critical alerts must be acknowledged within 15 minutes, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Procedure: 1) Acknowledge the alert in the monitoring console and open an incident ticket. 2) Check whether related alerts exist for the same server, network segment or application. 3) Follow the matching troubleshooting procedure for the alert type. 4) If the cause is not known within 30 minutes, escalate to the Incident Manager. 5) Close the alert only after the metric returns to normal and the ticket notes are complete.

Title: Critical infrastructure incident escalation
Description: A critical infrastructure incident is an outage of a production service, an outage affecting more than one site, or any event that puts data at risk.
Procedure: 1) Declare the incident as critical in the ticketing system within 15 minutes of detection. 2) Notify the on-call Incident Manager by phone, not only by email. 3) The Incident Manager assigns a technical lead and opens a bridge call. 4) Escalate to the IT Operations Manager if service is not restored within 1 hour. 5) Escalate to the IT Director if service is not restored within 4 hours or if data loss is suspected. 6) Send stakeholder updates every 30 minutes until closure.
Escalation: Incident Manager on-call, then IT Operations Manager, then IT Director

Title: Application downtime response
Description: Application downtime means users cannot complete core business transactions. The first goal is to confirm the outage and find the affected users.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the outage with a test transaction and identify the affected users. 2) Check the application health page, the application server status and database connectivity. 3) Check change requests and deployments made in the last 24 hours. 4) If a recent change caused the outage, follow the approved rollback plan. 5) Log the start time, impact and actions in the incident ticket. 6) Escalate to the Incident Manager if the application is not restored within 30 minutes.
Escalation: Application Support on-call, then Incident Manager

Title: Network latency investigation
Description: Network latency is considered high when round-trip time between sites or to a service stays above 150 milliseconds, or when packet loss is above 1 percent.
Procedure: 1) Measure round-trip time and packet loss with ping from the affected client and from the server. 2) Check whether latency is high for all users or only one site or application. 3) Check WAN link utilization on the network monitoring dashboard. 4) Look for interface errors or discards on the core and edge switches. 5) If the WAN link stays above 85 percent utilization for 15 minutes, raise a capacity review with the Network team.

Title: Disk failure response
Description: A disk failure is reported when the RAID controller or server hardware monitoring shows a failed disk or a disk with a predicted failure.
Procedure: 1) Confirm the failed disk slot, serial number and array status in the hardware management console. 2) Check that the RAID array is running in a degraded state and is not offline. 3) Raise a hardware replacement request for the approved spare part. 4) Replace the disk only when the hardware technician is on site, using the approved hot swap procedure. 5) Confirm the array rebuild completes and record the rebuild time in the ticket.

Title: Patch management cycle
Description: Security patches are applied monthly on the second Tuesday of the month. Critical security patches must be applied within 14 days of release.
Procedure: 1) Download the patch list and classify each patch by severity. 2) Test the patches on the staging server group for at least three days. 3) Schedule production patching in the approved maintenance window. 4) Reboot servers only when the patch requires it, then confirm all services are running. 5) Record the patch results and any failed servers in the patch report.

Title: Security incident reporting
Description: Any suspected security incident, including malware, phishing, unauthorised login or data exposure, must be reported immediately.
Procedure: 1) Do not switch off or change the affected system unless it is causing active harm, so that evidence is preserved. 2) Report the incident to the Security Operations Centre (SOC) by phone within 30 minutes of detection. 3) Record the time, user, system and symptoms in the security ticket. 4) Isolate the network port only when the SOC advises. 5) Follow SOC instructions for the rest of the response.

Title: Service availability reporting
Description: Service availability is measured monthly for each production service against the agreed target of 99.5 percent.
Procedure: 1) Export the uptime data for each service from the monitoring tool on the first working day of the month. 2) Subtract planned maintenance minutes approved in change requests. 3) Calculate availability as uptime divided by the total minutes in the month minus planned maintenance minutes. 4) Report any service below 99.5 percent to the IT Operations Manager with the related incident references.

Title: Log analysis for troubleshooting
Description: Logs from servers, applications and network devices are sent to the central log platform and kept for 90 days.
Procedure: 1) Filter logs by the affected host name and the incident time window, starting 15 minutes before the first alert. 2) Search for error, critical and failed login messages. 3) Compare the first error with recent change records. 4) Attach the relevant log extract to the incident ticket. Do not copy logs that contain personal data outside the central log platform.

Title: Storage pool utilization above 85 percent
Description: Shared storage pools (SAN or NAS) should stay below 85 percent utilization to leave room for growth and snapshots.
Procedure: 1) Identify the largest volumes and projects on the storage management console. 2) Check whether snapshot retention or old backup copies are consuming space. 3) Remove only data approved for deletion by the data owner. 4) If usage is still above 85 percent after cleanup, raise a capacity request for additional storage.

Title: Disaster recovery plan activation
Description: The disaster recovery (DR) plan is activated when a primary data centre outage is expected to last more than 8 hours, or when a major data loss affects a core system.
Procedure: 1) The Incident Manager confirms the DR declaration with the IT Director. 2) Start the DR runbook for the affected system at the DR site. 3) Confirm the most recent replicated data point and record the recovery point. 4) Notify business owners of the expected recovery time. 5) Test DR services at least twice a year and record the results in the DR report.
Escalation: Disaster Recovery Coordinator, then IT Director

Title: Planned infrastructure maintenance
Description: Planned maintenance runs in the approved window of Saturday 22:00 to Sunday 04:00, unless the Change Advisory Board approves another time.
Procedure: 1) Raise a change request at least five working days before the window. 2) Notify users and the service desk at least two working days before the window. 3) Take a verified backup before any change to a production server. 4) Run the change steps in order and record each step result. 5) Confirm services and monitoring after the change, then close the change record.

Title: Network interface errors and packet discards
Description: Rising interface error counters and discards usually point to a damaged cable, a faulty optic or a duplex mismatch.
Procedure: 1) Check CRC errors, input errors and output discards on the switch or router interface. 2) Replace the patch cable or optic if CRC errors keep increasing. 3) Check that both ends of the link use auto negotiation, or the same speed and duplex. 4) Monitor the port for 30 minutes after the change.

Title: High disk utilization on a server volume
Description: A server volume above 90 percent used can stop applications from writing logs and data. Work through the steps in order and never delete application data without approval.
Procedure: 1) Identify the volume and the largest folders using the disk analysis tool. 2) Check whether log files, temporary files or old backup files are the cause. 3) Compress or move log files older than 30 days to the archive location, as approved by the application owner. 4) Do not delete application data or database files without owner approval. 5) If free space remains below 10 percent after cleanup, raise a storage capacity request.

Title: Application fails to start after restart
Description: An application may fail to start after a restart because of a stale lock file, a missing configuration file or a dependent service that has not started yet.
Procedure: 1) Read the application start-up log and find the first error. 2) Check that the dependent database and message queue services are running. 3) Check for stale lock or PID files and remove them only after confirming no process is running. 4) Confirm the configuration file was not changed outside an approved change window. 5) If the application still does not start, escalate to the Application Support on-call team.

Title: Critical incident stakeholder communication
Description: Stakeholders must receive clear and regular updates during a critical incident so that business teams can plan their response.
Procedure: 1) Send the first notice within 30 minutes of declaring a critical incident, using the approved template. 2) Include the affected service, the business impact, the start time and the time of the next update. 3) Send updates every 30 minutes until service is restored. 4) Send a closure notice with the root cause summary and follow-up actions within 2 working days.
